title: Equivalent Fractions for Grade 4: The Same-Number Rule Made Simple + Free Quiz
meta_title: Equivalent Fractions Grade 4: Rules + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master equivalent fractions grade 4 with fraction bars, the same-number rule, missing numerators, simplifying and comparing, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Two fractions can look completely different and still mean the same amount. Here is how I teach equivalent fractions to Grade 4 — fraction bars, the same-number rule, and a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Cut a roti in half, then slice each half again — you now hold four pieces, and two of them make exactly the same amount as the single big half you started with. That picture is the whole idea behind equivalent fractions grade 4 children need to carry into the rest of primary maths. Two fractions are equivalent when they name the same amount even though the numbers look different: 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8 are three ways of writing one idea. Once a child truly sees that, comparing and ordering fractions stops being guesswork.

I have taught this to plenty of nine-year-olds, and the mistake is always the same — they judge a fraction by its numbers instead of the amount it stands for. So we start with pictures, then earn the rule.

What makes two fractions equal

Draw two identical bars. Shade half of the first. Under it, draw the same bar split into four and shade two of those parts. The shaded lengths line up exactly. Nothing was added or taken away — the second bar just chopped the same amount into more, smaller pieces. That is the definition worth repeating: same amount, different numbers.

This is why 1/2 and 50/100 are equal, and why 3/3, 5/5 and 8/8 all equal one whole. Get a child to prove two fractions equal with a drawing before they ever touch a rule, and the rule makes sense instead of feeling like magic.

The same-number rule: multiply or divide the top and bottom together

Here is the rule that runs the whole topic. To make an equivalent fraction, multiply or divide the numerator and the denominator by the same number — never a different one for each.

Multiplying up

Start with 3/4. Multiply top and bottom by 2 and you get 6/8. Multiply the original by 3 and you get 9/12. All three are the same amount because multiplying top and bottom by the same number is just cutting each piece into more parts — it does not change how much is shaded.

Dividing down

The rule runs backwards too. Take 6/8, divide top and bottom by 2, and you land back on 3/4. Dividing only works when both numbers share a common factor, which is exactly what makes simplifying possible.

Finding a missing numerator or denominator

Grade 4 papers love a gap: 2/3 = ?/12. The trick is to ask what happened to the denominator. 3 became 12, so it was multiplied by 4. The same-number rule says do the identical thing to the top: 2 × 4 = 8. So 2/3 = 8/12. If the gap is on the bottom — say 5/6 = 20/? — look at the numerator first: 5 became 20, a multiply by 4, so the bottom is 6 × 4 = 24.

One honest caveat I always share: the ‘what did I multiply by’ jump only works when the numbers divide cleanly. If 3 does not go neatly into the number given, the pair is not equivalent, and that is a perfectly valid answer to circle.

Simplifying a fraction to lowest terms

Simplifying is just the dividing-down rule used until you cannot go further. Take 8/12. Both 8 and 12 divide by 4, giving 2/3. Since 2 and 3 share no common factor bigger than 1, 2/3 is the lowest term — the simplest name for that amount.

My tip: hunt for the biggest number that divides both at once rather than chipping away by 2 repeatedly. 12/18 both divide by 6 straight to 2/3. Chipping by 2 gets you 6/9, then you still have to divide by 3. Fewer steps, fewer slips.

Comparing fractions by making equivalent ones

This is where equivalent fractions earns its keep. Which is bigger, 2/3 or 3/4? You cannot compare thirds against fourths directly, so rewrite both with the same denominator. Twelfths work for both: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Now it is obvious — 9/12 beats 8/12, so 3/4 is larger.

TaskWhat you doExample
Make an equivalent fractionMultiply top and bottom by the same number3/4 = 6/8
Find a missing numberSpot the multiply, copy it to the other part2/3 = 8/12
SimplifyDivide top and bottom by their biggest common factor8/12 = 2/3
Compare two fractionsRewrite both with the same denominator2/3 < 3/4

A quick checklist before your child says done

  • Did I do the same thing to the top and the bottom?
  • Can this answer still be simplified — do the two numbers share a factor?
  • For a comparison, are both fractions written over the same denominator?
  • Does a quick bar drawing agree with my numbers?

Work through that list and most careless errors vanish. Speed comes later; right now the aim is a child who can explain why 2/4 and 1/2 are the same rather than just chanting it.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz covering exactly what we walked through — spotting equal fractions, the same-number rule, missing numbers, simplifying and comparing. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for any they miss. When they want more written practice, the printable worksheet at the end gives graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Equivalent Fractions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on equal fractions, the same-number rule, missing numbers, simplifying and comparing. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.explanation: Multiply top and bottom of 1/2 by 2 to get 2/4, so they name the same amount.
The bottom 4 became 8, a multiply by 2, so the top must also double: 3 x 2 = 6.
Both 6 and 9 divide by 3, giving 2/3, which cannot be reduced further.

questions.q: Which pair of fractions is equivalent?
questions.explanation: Multiply 3/5 top and bottom by 2 to get 6/10, so the pair is equivalent.
The top 2 became 8, a multiply by 4, so the bottom is 3 x 4 = 12.
Rewrite both over 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12, so 3/4 is larger.

questions.q: What is 5/10 in its simplest form?
questions.explanation: Both 5 and 10 divide by 5, giving 1/2, the simplest name for that amount.

questions.q: To make an equivalent fraction, what must you do?
options: Add the same number to top and bottom
Multiply top and bottom by the same number
questions.explanation: Multiplying (or dividing) both the numerator and denominator by the same number keeps the amount the same.

faq.q: What are equivalent fractions in Grade 4?
faq.a: They are fractions that show the same amount using different numbers, such as 1/2, 2/4 and 4/8. In Grade 4 children learn to make, check and simplify them using the same-number rule.

faq.q: Why do you multiply the top and bottom by the same number?
faq.a: Because multiplying both parts by the same number only cuts each piece into more, smaller pieces — the total shaded amount stays exactly the same, so the fraction’s value does not change.

faq.q: How do you find a missing numerator or denominator?
faq.a: Look at the part that changed and work out what it was multiplied by, then do the identical thing to the other part. For 2/3 = ?/12, the bottom was multiplied by 4, so the top is 2 × 4 = 8.

faq.q: How do you simplify a fraction to lowest terms?
faq.a: Divide the numerator and denominator by their biggest common factor. For 8/12, both divide by 4 to give 2/3, which cannot be reduced any further.
